item.title: AI can search for consensus protocols, but who checks the search?
item.description:
Replicated databases need nearby reads without letting different copies tell incompatible stories. The paper gives a concrete failure in Bodega: a responder returns a newly accepted value of 7, then a later read at the leader returns absence because its commit messages are delayed. Agreement on writes is not enough if read paths expose different stages of that agreement.

Burgelin and colleagues propose AI-greement, an environment in which a coding agent designs, implements, benchmarks, and formalizes consensus protocols. Its output, A-greement, improves mean latency in the evaluated deployments, but human review still removed an inherited flaw and a benchmark exploit. The central lesson is that performance feedback, model proofs, and expert review protect different boundaries and cannot replace one another.

item.title: Fewer consensus messages can still mean slower agreement
item.description:
A group of servers agreeing on a shared ledger can waste time in opposite ways. One design makes everyone exchange votes, keeping the network busy; another funnels votes through a leader, which can become the slowest worker. A timer adds another trap: setting it too short can restart work that was about to finish, while setting it too long delays recovery from a crashed leader.

This paper proposes simple equations for understanding those interactions in HotStuff and Istanbul BFT , or IBFT . Its central lesson is that consensus latency depends on where messages accumulate and which operations must wait for one another, so fewer total messages need not produce faster agreement. Beyond blockchains, this suggests a useful way to read distributed-system performance claims: ask which resource must do the work, not just how much work exists overall.

item.title: Narwhal and Tusk: Moving the Bottleneck Out of BFT Consensus
item.description: For most of the last decade, work on fast Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) consensus has focused on one number: message complexity, meaning how many protocol messages the validators exchange per decision. HotStuff (Yin et al., 2019) brought that number down to linear in the partially synchronous setting by routing all votes through a leader. The paper by Danezis, Kokoris-Kogias, Sonnino and Spiegelman, published at EuroSys 2022, argues that this target misses where the cost actually sits in a real ledger. The expensive part is not agreeing on an order. It is moving the transactions themselves to every validator, reliably.

item.title: A BFT ordering service for Fabric, and the library under it
item.description: Fabric’s ordering service receives endorsed transactions from clients and emits a stream of blocks. When we wrote this paper the latest release, v2.3, ran it on Raft, which tolerates crashes and nothing worse. The paper describes how my co-authors and I made Fabric Byzantine fault-tolerant end to end: a consensus library in Go, based on the BFT-SMaRt protocol, and the changes to the orderer, the peer and the client that had to come with it.
